before: Maybe you've let a small child win at Go Fish and never found a good time to start playing for real. Who wants to be the grown-up who finally wins? Without the Guide, you can slide from looking after your little one into spoiling it the same way. Sweets and screens can pass for loving yourself, and so can getting it out of anything hard.
after: Once a need does show, after all that hiding, it's okay to want a lot of closeness. Then someone you love goes for a walk alone, and you've sent "hello??" before they've reached the corner. Look at how you're going about getting the need met, since demanding instant replies, or making someone pay for needing space, is another matter. The Guide helps you find a way that works for you both. But give the need a fair hearing first: I think your little one wants to know they're coming back.

guide_passage:
The r4 guide's passage (the passage this carries):
The opposite trap is forced adulthood: perfect discipline, no visible needs, and very little joy or closeness. In that case the next adult act may be asking for help, expressing a preference, or letting a safe person see something imperfect—not tightening control again.
brief:
- the meaning, in plain words: the opposite trap is forced adulthood: holding yourself to perfect discipline, never letting a need show, and very little joy or closeness. If you're stuck there, the next grown-up step may be asking someone safe for help, or saying what you'd like, not tightening your grip again.
- build the paragraph around ONE everyday example, and let it be a bit goofy, the way the article's humor is ("Don't be a silly rabbit!", "(NOT with a hammer!)", "you've sent "hello??" before they've reached the corner"), not sad or poignant. Then come back to it for the way out.
- name forced adulthood inside a sentence that's also doing something else (reacting, joking, or comparing it with P2's trap), not as a label sentence of its own like "That's forced adulthood, the opposite trap."
- the way out can be what the reader would actually say ("Could you grab the other end?"), or the article's own opinion ("I'd..."). One "may" or "might" is enough. The urge to tighten your grip again stays in, in your own words.
- context, not for the text: the two paragraphs around this one read Human in Pangram: P2 with one playful example and a question ("Maybe you've let a small child win at Go Fish and never found a good time to start playing for real. Who wants to be the grown-up who finally wins?"), and P4 with one joke and an opinion ("Then someone you love goes for a walk alone, and you've sent "hello??" before they've reached the corner." ... "I think your little one wants to know they're coming back."). All seven drafts of this paragraph read AI. Each stacked several sad, observed details (running in the sleet, a shelf leaning against the wall, the recovery room, a tooth nobody knows about, the hairdresser washing your hair, the dishes at a party, eating standing up), then a label sentence ("That's forced adulthood, the opposite trap."), then "the next grown-up step might be X. Or Y.", with "tighten your grip again". The closest to Human (0.46) had an opinion ("I think this one's harder to spot, since it looks so responsible.") and its two steps as quotes.
- context, not for the text: don't use "the next grown-up step", "tighten your grip", "That's forced adulthood", "If you're stuck there", "very little joy or closeness", "No wonder", or any of the examples above. When to Change the Strategy already has "texting a friend that you're having a rough day instead of saying you're fine", so not that or anything like it. P2 just used a child's card game and P4 a walk and a text; use something else.
